title: Reported questions, commands and requests
tagline: How to report what someone asked or told you to do, without the question mark.
why: Reporting what someone asked you, or what they told you to do, is essential for describing a real conversation — in a story, an email, or the Speaking Part 2 collaborative task where you explain what your partner suggested. B1 Preliminary checks that you can turn a direct question into a reported one (no question mark, no do/does/did) and that you know the right pattern after tell, ask, suggest and warn.

hook.text: Nadia missed the camping trip meeting. Liam: "Miss Vega asked if we had sleeping bags." Sofia: "And she told us to bring warm clothes." Nadia: "What did she ask about the food?"
hook.ask: Liam reports a yes/no question, and Sofia reports an instruction. Look at the word order after asked if — is it the same as a real question, or different?

diagrams.title: A question becomes a reported question

before.text: "Do you have a sleeping bag?" Miss Vega asked.

after.text: Miss Vega asked if I had a sleeping bag.

steps: Add if or whether — no question mark, no auxiliary do/does/did.
Change the word order back to statement order (subject before verb).
Move the tense back one step, just like reported statements.

rows.label: Word order
cells: infinitive with to — no subject needed

rows.label: Example
cells: She asked if I had a tent.
She told me to bring warm clothes.

rows.label: Negative
cells: She asked if I hadn't forgotten anything.
She told me not to forget my torch.

diagrams.title: How to report a wh- question

steps.label: Move the tense back and remove the question mark
steps.ex: She asked where we were going.

head: Type
Pattern
Example
rows: She asked if I had a tent.
She asked where we were meeting.
She told us to bring warm clothes.
She asked us not to be late.
She wanted us to arrive on time.
suggest + -ing; advise/warn/tell sb (not) to; promise/offer/refuse + to
She advised us to leave early. He refused to apologise.

examples.text: "Do you have a sleeping bag?" → She asked if I had a sleeping bag.
examples.note: no do, question word order becomes statement order

examples.text: "Are you coming on Saturday?" → He asked whether I was coming on Saturday.
examples.note: whether works just like if here

examples.text: "Have you packed yet?" → She asked if we had packed yet.
examples.note: the tense also moves back one step

examples.text: "Where are we meeting?" → She asked where we were meeting.
examples.note: keep the wh-word, statement order after it

examples.text: "What time does the bus leave?" → He asked what time the bus left.
examples.note: no does — just statement word order

examples.text: "Why is Nadia absent?" → Liam asked why Nadia was absent.
"Bring warm clothes." → She told us to bring warm clothes.
examples.note: an instruction: tell + person + to + verb

examples.text: "Don't forget your torch." → She told me not to forget my torch.
"Could you carry the tent, please?" → She asked me to carry the tent.
examples.note: a polite request reported the same way

examples.text: "Please don't be late." → She asked us not to be late.

use.point: Other reporting verbs: suggest, warn, promise, want

examples.text: "Let's take extra water," she said. → She suggested taking extra water.
"Be careful near the river," she said. → She warned us to be careful near the river.
"I'll bring the first-aid kit," she said. → She promised to bring the first-aid kit.
examples.note: promise + to + verb, no person needed

examples.text: Miss Vega wanted us to check the forecast before the trip.
examples.note: want sb (not) to + verb — the same pattern as ask/tell

watch_out.wrong: She asked if did I have a tent.
watch_out.right: She asked if I had a tent.
watch_out.why: No do/did and no question word order after if — it goes back to statement order.

watch_out.wrong: She asked where were we meeting.
watch_out.why: Subject before verb after the wh-word — not question order.

watch_out.wrong: She told to us bring warm clothes.
watch_out.right: She told us to bring warm clothes.
watch_out.why: tell + person, then to + verb — no to before the person.

watch_out.wrong: She asked us don't be late.
watch_out.right: She asked us not to be late.
watch_out.why: The negative in a reported command is not to + verb, not don't.

watch_out.wrong: She suggested to take extra water.
watch_out.why: suggest is followed by the -ing form, never to + verb.

watch_out.wrong: She asked if I have packed yet?
watch_out.right: She asked if I had packed yet.
watch_out.why: No question mark in reported speech, and the tense moves back too.

l1.es: Me preguntó si tenía una carpa.
l1.wrong: She asked me if did I have a tent.
l1.right: She asked me if I had a tent.
l1.why: Spanish keeps normal word order after si; copy that in English — no do/did after if.

l1.es: Me dijo que trajera ropa de abrigo.
l1.wrong: She told that I bring warm clothes.
l1.right: She told me to bring warm clothes.
l1.why: tell needs a person straight after it, then to + verb — no that here.

l1.wrong: She asked me where were we.
l1.why: After a wh-word, English goes back to statement order, unlike a direct question.

l1.es: Me pidió que no llegara tarde.
l1.wrong: She asked me don't be late.
l1.right: She asked me not to be late.
l1.why: A reported negative request is ask sb not to + verb, not don't.

remember.trick: No question mark, no do — statement order, go!
remember.tip: Before you report a question, turn it into a statement in your head first — then add if, whether or the wh-word.

dialogue.title: What did she say?
dialogue.context: Nadia missed the meeting about the camping trip, so Mateo, Sofia and Liam report what Miss Vega asked and told them.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: I missed the whole meeting! What did she ask?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: She asked if everyone had a sleeping bag.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: And she asked whether we were bringing our own tents.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: OK. Did she tell us to bring anything special?

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: Yes — she told us to bring warm clothes and a torch.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: And she told me not to forget my medicine.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: She also suggested taking extra water for the hike.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: Thanks! Now I know what to pack.

can_do: I can report yes/no questions with ask if/whether + statement word order.
I can report wh- questions, keeping the wh-word but changing the word order.
I can report commands and requests with tell/ask/want sb (not) to, and other verbs like suggest, warn, advise, promise, offer and refuse.
summary: Reported questions lose the question mark and go back to statement word order — no do/does/did.
ask if / ask whether reports a yes/no question; keep the wh-word for a wh- question.
tell sb (not) to + verb reports a command; ask sb (not) to + verb reports a request.
suggest is followed by -ing, not to + verb — it's the odd one out.
warn, advise, promise and offer each have their own pattern — check the verb before you build the sentence.
